chapters.title: Read a Gesture Only After You Know the Person
chapters.hook: Your new boss sits through your idea with her arms crossed, eyes on the window. You're already planning to rewrite it all tonight.
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think folded arms or a look away means the same thing on anyone. Actually, a gesture only tells you something once you know how that person usually acts, because one person's warning sign is another person's everyday habit.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Before you judge any gesture, learn how the person normally acts when they feel relaxed.
chapters.tryThisNow: Choose one person you'll see today and note how they sit and talk when they're relaxed.

memorableLines.text: Know someone's normal first, and their gestures start to speak.

breakdown.fastRead:
Ten minutes into his Thursday update, Tomás watches his new boss, Ingrid, fold her arms and stare at the window. He is sure she hates the plan, and is ready to spend his weekend rebuilding it. He has known her for two weeks.

Folded arms and a look away don't mean the same thing on everyone. On one person they are a warning. On another they are a comfortable way to sit. Joe Navarro, a former FBI agent, says you can learn to read people. He tells of a police officer, McFadden, who saw from some men's behavior that they were sizing up a store for a crime. What he saw became the basis of a Supreme Court ruling. But before you read anyone, Navarro says, learn a person's baseline, meaning how they normally sit, talk and move when at ease. A change from that normal is what tells you something. Start with the people you live and work with.

Tomás keeps his plan. All week he watches Ingrid in meetings. She folds her arms and gazes out the window even while she praises the team. It is how she thinks, and now he would notice if it changed. Learn how a person acts when relaxed before you judge a gesture, and you will spot the changes that matter.

Joe Navarro was an FBI agent who worked in counterintelligence, the job of catching spies. He holds that anyone can learn to read people, and that most of what people tell each other is said without words. So he says to train yourself to watch. He tells of a police officer, McFadden, who saw from some men's behavior that they were sizing up a store to commit a crime. What he saw became the basis of a 1968 Supreme Court ruling, Terry v. Ohio. It lets police stop and pat down someone whose behavior shows they mean to commit a crime. Behavior, watched closely, can show what a person intends.

Navarro sets out ten rules for watching people well, and they come in a set order. First, be alert to everything around you. Second, read behavior in its setting, since where and when it happens changes what it means. Third, learn the universal signals, the ones nearly everyone shows. Fourth, learn each person's idiosyncratic signals, meaning the habits that belong to that person alone. Fifth, set a baseline, which is how the person normally sits, talks and moves when at ease.

Sixth, look for clusters of tells. A tell is any behavior that reveals what someone thinks or feels, and a cluster is several of them together. Seventh, watch for changes, since a change in behavior signals a change in thought, feeling or intent. Eighth, learn to spot false or misleading signals. Ninth, separate signs of comfort from signs of discomfort. Tenth, watch quietly, without making a show of it.

Look at how many of those rules lean on knowing the person. A cluster means little until you know which moves are normal for someone. A change only shows up against what came before. Navarro says several tells read together against a baseline are more accurate than one gesture read alone. The baseline is what turns his other rules into real readings instead of guesses.

That is why his advice for this week starts close to home. Watch the people you live and work with, and learn how they normally act before you judge anything they do. Notice how a partner sits at breakfast on an ordinary morning. Notice where a coworker looks when a meeting is going fine. These quiet moments give you something to compare against later. Then, when someone who always chatters goes silent, you will know it means something.

So Tomás keeps his plan and finishes the update. All week he watches Ingrid in other meetings. She folds her arms and gazes out the window even while she praises the team, and again while she laughs at a joke. It is simply how she thinks. Now he has something to compare against, and if she ever does something new, he will see it. Learn how a person acts when relaxed before you judge a gesture, and you will spot the changes that matter.

examples.title: A quiet seller in the Monday call
examples.scenario: Rosa has run a five-person sales team for a month. In Monday's sales call, she asks Dmitri about his biggest deal. He answers in two-word replies, clicking his pen and staring at his screen. Rosa's stomach drops, because if that deal slips, the team misses its target. Her cursor is in the forecast sheet, and she has to decide whether to mark his deal at risk.
examples.whatToDo: Leave the deal unmarked for now. Over the next few calls, notice how Dmitri talks when his deals are clearly going well.
examples.whyItMatters: If short answers and pen clicks are just his way, she avoids doubting a good seller over a habit.

examples.title: The lab partner who won't look up
examples.scenario: Amara, sixteen, read a list online saying that people who avoid your eyes are hiding something. Her new chemistry partner, Ji-ho, never looks at her when they talk. So she decided he disliked her and stopped sharing her notes. Then she saw him with his best friend, his eyes on the desk, laughing hard. Their last lab report came back with a C.
examples.whatToDo: Throw out the list and start over. Watch how Ji-ho acts when he's clearly at ease, and judge his eyes against that.
examples.whyItMatters: If looking down is just his habit, she stops punishing it and saves the partnership and the grade.

examples.title: Is his sister unhappy for him?
examples.scenario: Owen stands at his engagement dinner and toasts his fiancée. Across the table, his older sister, Carmen, sits with her arms folded and barely smiles. Owen's face goes hot. He has wanted her blessing for months. As everyone claps, he plans what to say to her in the hallway later. 'Could you at least pretend to be happy for me?'
examples.whatToDo: Before the hallway, think back to other family dinners. If Carmen sits like this whenever she's content, tonight's folded arms show nothing new.
examples.whyItMatters: He avoids picking a fight on his big night with a sister who may be quietly proud of him.

questions.prompt: You've just joined a book club. Every week one member, an older man, sits with his arms tightly crossed while others share. You want to know if he dislikes the group. What do you do?
choices: Watch how he sits on nights when he is laughing and joining in.
Uncross your own arms and smile at him to help put him at ease.
Ask the club's host whether he has seemed unhappy in recent weeks.
questions.explanation: His crossed arms only mean something next to how he sits when he's clearly enjoying himself. Asking the host just gets another guess about the same arms, with nothing to compare them to.

questions.prompt: On her first shift with a new patient, a nurse takes his pain history. He looks at the floor the whole time, so she writes 'may be exaggerating' in his chart. What trap did she fall into?
choices: Writing a guess in the chart where other staff would read it.
Watching his eyes when she should have trusted his words.
Reading his downward eyes before she knew how he usually looks.
questions.explanation: She had just met him, so she had no idea how he looks when he's at ease. Looking down may simply be his habit. Ignoring his eyes would only throw away a skill worth learning.

questions.prompt: A new team lead spends her first two weeks noticing how each person acts in ordinary meetings. One engineer is always chatty. In week three, when a deadline comes up, he goes silent and stares at his laptop. What is most likely to happen next?
choices: She stays unsure, since silence can mean very different things for different people.
She spots the change at once and asks him about the deadline.
She misses it, since one quiet person is easy to overlook.
questions.explanation: She already knows he's normally chatty, so his silence is a change from his usual self, and a change is what tells her something. Staying unsure would make sense only with a stranger.

questions.prompt: Your friend says, "My new roommate sits with her arms crossed every time we talk in the kitchen. She clearly can't stand me." What's the best thing to tell your friend?
choices: "Ask her straight out tonight whether something about you is bothering her."
"Watch how she sits with friends she likes before deciding that."
"Look up what crossed arms usually mean, to be sure."
questions.explanation: Crossed arms may just be how she sits. Watching her with friends she likes shows her relaxed normal, so you can tell if the kitchen is different. A general meaning can't tell you what they mean on her.

questions.prompt: A girl is usually loud and joking at breakfast. On the morning of a school trip, she eats in silence. Her father asks about the trip, and she admits she's nervous. Why did his reading of her work?
choices: He knew her normal mornings, so the silence stood out as a change.
Silence at breakfast is a sign of nerves in nearly every child.
He asked her about it directly rather than trying to guess from her face.
questions.explanation: He knew how she acts on a normal morning, loud and joking. Against that, silence was a real change worth asking about. On a child he didn't know, silence could mean anything.

questions.prompt: On your first shift as the new manager of a small café, one barista gives you one-word answers and avoids your eyes. You'll be working with her five days a week. What's your move this week?
choices: Decide she resents having a new boss, and keep your distance for now.
Watch today for more signs of resentment before you decide anything.
Spend the week seeing how she acts with regulars she clearly likes.
questions.explanation: One morning with a new boss shows little about her normal. Watching her with regulars she likes shows how she acts at ease. More signs today would only stack guesses on a first impression.

questions.prompt: Before a job interview, a man reads an article on body language. When the interviewer leans back and touches her chin, he decides she's bored, and his confidence sinks. He doesn't get the job. Where did he go wrong?
choices: Judging her lean and chin touch with no idea how she usually sits.
Reading an article about body language in the hour before his big job interview.
Deciding from two small signs instead of waiting to see several more.
questions.explanation: He had just met her, so a lean and a chin touch had nothing to compare against. How she sat during the first small talk would have shown her normal. More signs read the same way wouldn't help.

reviewCards.front: Your new neighbor never smiles when you say hello in the stairwell, and you start to think they dislike you.
reviewCards.back: Hold off on deciding. Notice how they act with people they're clearly easy around, then judge the missing smile against that.

reviewCards.front: Why can't you tell what a stranger's folded arms mean at a glance?
reviewCards.back: Because the same move can be one person's everyday habit and another's warning sign. Without their relaxed normal, you have nothing to compare it to.

reviewCards.front: Before you decide what a coworker's long sigh means, first find out ...
reviewCards.back: ... how that coworker acts on a calm, ordinary day, so you can tell whether the sigh is new.

reviewCards.front: A coach benched a quiet new player for a bad attitude because he never looked up during team talks. A week later she saw him look down even while joking with friends.
reviewCards.back: She judged his eyes before she knew his normal. Looking down was just his habit, so she punished a habit instead of a mood.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what should you do before reading meaning into someone's gesture?
reviewCards.back: Learn how they act when they're relaxed. A gesture tells you something when it's a change from that.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Get to know someone's everyday, at-ease way of moving and talking, so a real change stands out from a habit.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I sit down to eat with someone I live or work with, I notice one thing about how they sit, talk or move while they're relaxed.
When I catch myself guessing what someone's gesture means, I ask whether I've seen them do it when relaxed, and wait to judge until I know.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before tonight, think of one gesture you read into lately, like a sigh or a look away. Ask yourself whether that person does it on calm days too.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each evening this week, write one line about how a person you live or work with acts when relaxed. On Sunday, read the lines and pick out which moves are simply their habits.

chapters.title: Why Hands Fly to the Neck After a Hard Question
chapters.hook: You ask a hard question and get a calm no. The hand that drifts to their throat a second later is harder to fake.
chapters.counterintuition: It feels natural to shrug off a hand on the neck as an itch or a habit. But a touch right after a question shows the question stung, because the brain's alarm reacts and the body calms itself before anyone can think to hide it.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When someone touches their neck or face right after a question, that question just made them uneasy.
chapters.tryThisNow: Put your phone in a pocket before your next conversation today, and watch the other person's hands and neck while they answer.

memorableLines.text: The hand that rushes to the neck tells you which question hurt.

breakdown.fastRead:
Why would a hand fly to someone's throat the instant you ask them something? Joe Navarro reads that hand as an answer. He points to the limbic system, the part of the brain that reacts to danger at once, without stopping to think. A hard question can feel like danger. The body then reaches for a pacifying behavior, a small touch that calms it. Think of rubbing the neck, stroking the face or smoothing the hair. These moves are wired in for survival, so they show up before anyone can decide to hide them.

Navarro tells of agents hunting a man on the run. They questioned a woman at a house. Each time they asked whether he could be inside, she said no. Each time, her hand went up to cover the small hollow at the base of her throat. The agents searched the house and found him there. Navarro counts the neck among the most telling places to watch.

Most people would call her touch an itch, and the clue would be lost. An itch can come at any moment, but her hand rose with the same question every time. Once you watch the hands right after you ask, you know which question made the other person uneasy.

Why would a hand fly to someone's throat the instant you ask them something? Joe Navarro reads that hand as an answer. Most people never notice it, and the few who do shrug and move on. To see why it matters, start inside the head.

Navarro points to the limbic system, the part of the brain that reacts to danger at once, without stopping to think. He calls it the honest brain. The neocortex, the thinking brain on top, can plan a story and tell a lie. The limbic system has no time for that. It is wired in for survival, so it fires before we can think to hide what it does. That is why its signals are so honest.

Its reactions come in a set order. First comes freeze. A person under threat goes still, so as not to be noticed. Next comes flight, getting away. In an office or a kitchen you rarely run, so the body blocks instead. People close or cover their eyes, lean away, or put an object between themselves and the other person. Last comes fight. Today that seldom means fists. It shows up as arguing, insults or pushing into someone's space.

Once the jolt passes, the body has to settle. It does so with pacifying behaviors, small self-touches that calm us after stress. People rub the neck, the face or the hair. They stroke their legs. They puff out their cheeks and let the air out slowly. Some pull a collar away from the neck, which Navarro calls ventilating. Each move is the brain soothing itself, and none of it is planned.

Navarro counts neck touching among the most telling of these. Men tend to grip or rub the neck. Women tend to cover the neck dimple, the small hollow at the base of the throat.

Navarro tells of agents hunting a man on the run. They questioned a woman at a house. Each time they asked whether he could be inside, she said no. Each time, her hand went up and covered her neck dimple. Her answer never changed, and neither did her hand. The agents searched the house and found him there.

Most people would call that touch an itch or a nervous habit, and the clue would be lost. An itch can come at any moment. Navarro's advice is to treat a self-touch that shows up right after a question or an event as a sign that something just caused discomfort. Context and timing do the work. Know how a person usually acts, so you can spot the change. A friend who twists her hair all evening tells you little by twisting it once more. A man who sat still until one question, then rubbed his neck, tells you a great deal.

So the hand at the throat is no accident. The honest brain moves first, and the hand points back at whatever just stung. Her hand rose with the same question every time, and that was the whole message. Once you watch the hands right after you ask, you know which question made the other person uneasy.

examples.title: Splitting the bill for a canoe weekend
examples.scenario: Dario is booking a canoe weekend for four friends. Over pizza, he asks if the tents work, if the snack plan works, and if $140 each works. Yuki laughs through the first two. At the price, she says, "Totally fine," and her fingers slide to the hollow of her throat. The deposit page is open on Dario's phone, his thumb over the pay button.
examples.whatToDo: Hold off on paying. Later, ask Yuki on her own how the $140 sits with her, and whether a cheaper site would help.
examples.whyItMatters: Her hand moved only at the price, so money is the sore spot. Asking now beats finding out after everyone has paid.

examples.title: A 6 a.m. shift nobody questioned
examples.scenario: Rafael runs a small bakery-cafe. Before setting the new schedule, he did the sensible thing and asked straight out: "Any problem opening alone at 6 a.m.?" His new barista, Femi, said, "No problem," rubbing the side of his neck hard. Rafael took him at his word. Two weeks later Femi quit, saying the first bus never got him in on time.
examples.whatToDo: When a yes comes with a hand on the neck, stay on that question and ask what would make the early shift work.
examples.whyItMatters: Asking straight out was fine. Missing the touch right after the question cost Rafael a good barista and a hole in the schedule.

examples.title: A supervisor who wants to move on
examples.scenario: Nadia is a nursing student on her first hospital placement. She asks an older patient, Henrik, if he takes his heart pills every day. "Every day," he says, and rubs the back of his neck. Her supervisor, Gloria, is already at the door. "People touch their necks all day, Nadia. He said yes. Next patient."
examples.whatToDo: Tell Gloria the rub came right after the pill question, then ask Henrik gently how the pills go on a busy day.
examples.whyItMatters: A touch at that exact moment points to the pills, and a missed dose matters more than one extra minute.

questions.prompt: Over lunch, you ask your brother if he's still fine lending you his car for your move. "Of course," he says, rubbing the back of his neck. He's been yawning all through lunch, so you put it down to a long day. What's the trap here?
choices: Asking him a yes-or-no question that let him off with an easy yes
Blaming the neck rub on tiredness when it came after the car question
Raising the car on a day he was clearly worn out
questions.explanation: The neck rub came just as the car came up, so that question made him uneasy. His tiredness was there all through lunch and doesn't explain the timing. A better day wouldn't help if the touch still got waved away.

questions.prompt: At a parents' evening, a teacher asks if the class trip's bus time works, if the packed lunch works, and if the cost works. One father nods each time but rubs his neck at the cost. If she talks with him later, what will she most likely find?
choices: That the cost is the part of the trip worrying him
That he's unhappy with the whole trip, bus included
That he has a stiff neck from a long day at work
questions.explanation: His hand moved only when the cost came up, so that question made him uneasy. The bus and the lunch got nods and no touch. A stiff neck wouldn't pick that exact moment to act up.

questions.prompt: Your friend runs a dog-walking business. She tells you, "I asked a client if my new prices were okay. He said yes, but rubbed his jaw the second I named them. Probably just an itch." What's your best reply?
choices: "Email him the new price list tonight so the whole deal is in writing."
"Ask him straight out again whether he's truly fine with them."
"The rub came with the prices, so ask what worries him about them."
questions.explanation: His hand went to his jaw right as the prices came up, so the prices are what bother him. Asking about his worry opens that up. Asking the same yes-or-no again likely gets the same polite yes.

questions.prompt: A hotel manager asks a cleaner about a guest's missing watch. Questions about her shift get calm, easy answers. Asked if she went into room 12, she says no and strokes her neck. The manager asks gently about room 12 and learns what happened. Why did watching her hand help?
choices: Her hand moved right after the room 12 question and after no other
A hand on the neck proved she had taken the watch from room 12
The calm early questions relaxed her, so her body stopped hiding
questions.explanation: Her hand rose right after the room 12 question, so that was the topic to follow. It showed unease about that room, not proof she took the watch. The gentle questions about room 12 did the rest.

questions.prompt: You're meeting someone who wants to rent your spare room. You ask about their last place, their job, and whether they've ever paid rent late. At the last one they rub their forehead and say, "Never." What's your next move?
choices: Move on to your next question and see if the touch comes back
Stay on rent a little longer and ask about their tight months
Lighten things up with a joke to put them at ease
questions.explanation: The forehead rub came right after the rent question, so that topic made them uneasy. Staying there gives you the chance to learn why. Moving on leaves the one clue you got behind you.

questions.prompt: In a job interview, you ask a candidate about her last boss, and she answers calmly. Ten minutes later, while you chat about parking, she rubs her neck. You mark her down for hiding trouble with that boss. Where did your thinking slip?
choices: Raising her old boss before she'd had any time to settle in
Chatting about parking when there were real questions to ask
Pinning a touch from the parking chat on the boss question
questions.explanation: The rub came ten minutes after the boss question, in the middle of talk about parking. A touch points to what just happened, not to something long past. Asking about her boss early was never the problem.

questions.prompt: At dinner, a teenager says his exams went fine. When his dad mentions the math results come out Friday, the boy rubs the back of his neck and reaches for the bread. Later his mom asks him only about math. What most likely happens when she asks?
choices: He talks about exams in general and math never comes up
He opens up about math, the subject he skipped past at dinner
He feels caught out and goes quiet about school for a few weeks
questions.explanation: His hand went to his neck right as the math results came up, so math is what made him uneasy. Asking only about math goes straight there. Talk of exams in general would let it slip past again.

reviewCards.front: A friend agrees to look after your cat for a week, then rubs the side of her neck. Why does it matter that the rub came right then?
reviewCards.back: Because a soothing touch follows whatever just made someone uneasy. Coming straight after your request, it points to the request as the thing bothering her.

reviewCards.front: When a hand goes to someone's neck or face just after you ask something, the topic to come back to is ...
reviewCards.back: ... the one you just asked about, because that question is the one that made them uneasy.

reviewCards.front: A tutor asked a student if last night's homework made sense. He said yes and smoothed his hair hard. The tutor moved on, and the next test showed he was lost.
reviewCards.back: The tutor took the yes and ignored the hand. The touch right after that question showed the homework troubled him, and a few more questions would have found the gap.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what does a hand at someone's neck or face tell you right after you ask them something?
reviewCards.back: That my question hit a sore spot. It isn't a random itch. Their body is calming itself, so that's the topic to stay with.

reviewCards.front: At a garage, you ask if your brakes will be fixed by Friday. The mechanic says "Sure" and rubs his jaw.
reviewCards.back: Stay on Friday. Ask what could slow the job down, so you hear about a delay now instead of on Friday morning.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Tying a hand at the neck or face to the exact question that came just before it.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I catch myself thinking a hand at someone's neck means nothing, I recall the question I asked just before and gently ask more about it.
When I sit down across from someone to ask something that matters, I put my phone away and watch their hands and neck right after each question.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the day ends, ask someone close to you a few easy questions and one that matters to them. Notice whether a hand goes to the neck or face, and after which question.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each time you arrive at a meeting, a class or a family meal this week, pick one person to watch. When a hand goes to their neck or face, recall the question that came just before it.

chapters.title: Trust the Feet When the Smile Says Stay
chapters.hook: You tell yourself a warm smile means the talk is going well. Meanwhile, under the table, their shoes have already turned toward the door.
chapters.counterintuition: You have probably been told that the face shows what someone really feels. The trouble is that people learn from childhood to manage their faces but almost never their feet, so look down first to see whether they want to stay.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When someone's feet turn toward the door, they want to leave, even while their face keeps smiling.
chapters.tryThisNow: Glance at one person's feet as you talk today, and if they turn toward the door, finish your point and offer to pick up later.

memorableLines.text: The face is trained to smile; the feet still point where they want to go.

breakdown.fastRead:
When a face and a pair of feet disagree, believe the feet. Joe Navarro calls the feet and legs the most honest part of the body. Ines, a photographer, is showing her prints to a café owner, hoping he will buy six for his walls. He smiles at every one. Yet his shoes have swung toward the kitchen door. Now both hands rest on his knees as he leans forward. Navarro calls this the knee clasp, a sign someone is ready to end the meeting.

We trust faces because that is where we look. It is also the part people practice. From childhood we learn to manage our faces, but almost no one learns to steer their feet. Feet were built to carry us away from danger. When a person wants out of a talk, the feet often turn toward the exit before the mouth says a word.

So Ines looks for a change. When she sat down, his feet faced her. Now they face the kitchen, and his hands on his knees say the same thing. She stops, leaves two prints and asks to come back on Friday. Pushing on would have lost the sale. Stop taking a smile as proof someone wants to stay, and let feet turned toward the door tell you when to finish.

We trust faces because that is where we look. It is also the part people practice. From childhood we learn to manage our faces. We smile at a dull gift, look calm when a teacher scolds us and look interested when we are bored. Almost no one is ever taught to mind their feet. So the face turns into a polite cover, and the feet are left to show what we really feel.

There is a reason the feet are so honest. Navarro links much of our body language to the limbic system, the old, fast part of the brain that reacts to danger before we stop to think. Feet were built to carry us away from trouble. When a person wants out of a talk, the feet often turn toward the exit before the mouth says a word. A second sign is the knee clasp. Both hands land on the knees and the weight shifts forward, ready to stand. The body is preparing to leave while the face is still being kind.

Reading feet still takes care, and Navarro's method keeps it from turning into guesswork. First, know how the person normally sits or stands, which he calls their baseline. Some people sit sideways out of habit, and some chairs simply face a door. Next, look for a change from that baseline, since a change is what carries the message. Then look for signs that agree. One sign can mislead you. Two that point the same way are much harder to argue with.

The same truth shows up when you join people. Walk up to two coworkers deep in a chat. If they turn their heads and shoulders to greet you but their feet stay pointed at each other, they would rather you did not join them. At home, a teenager may nod through a talk at the dinner table with both feet aimed at the stairs. Each time, the polite part of the body faces you, and the honest part faces where the person wants to be.

So Ines runs the method. When she sat down, the owner's feet faced her, and that was his baseline. Now they face the kitchen, a clear change. His hands on his knees agree with his feet. She finishes her sentence, leaves two prints on the table and asks to come back on Friday. He walks her to the door, warmer than he has been all afternoon. Pushing on would have lost the sale. Stop taking a smile as proof someone wants to stay, and let feet turned toward the door tell you when to finish.

examples.title: A boiler quote that runs long
examples.scenario: Kwame has just fixed a leaking boiler and is now explaining why the whole heating system should be replaced. The homeowner smiles and nods at each point. When he started, she faced him across the hallway. Now her slippers point toward the living room, where her phone keeps buzzing. Kwame has three more reasons on his clipboard, and a big job riding on them.
examples.whatToDo: Stop after the point he is on, hand her the written quote, and ask when she has ten minutes to go through it.
examples.whyItMatters: Her slippers have already left for the living room. Letting her go now keeps her goodwill, and the big job with it.

examples.title: The neighbour who smiled and said yes
examples.scenario: Ngozi runs the residents' group for her block. Tonight she needs a helper for the summer party and stops Pavel in the hallway. When she starts, he faces her. As she goes through the list of jobs, he keeps smiling and saying of course, but his feet have turned toward the stairwell. She still has half the list to go.
examples.whatToDo: Stop listing jobs, ask him for the one she needs most, and offer to go through the rest another evening.
examples.whyItMatters: His feet faced her at the start and have since turned to the stairs, so he wants to go. A short ask now keeps his goodwill for the rest.

examples.title: Twenty minutes into a guitar lesson
examples.scenario: Lucía teaches guitar to Oskar, sixteen, in her front room, where his stool faces the door. Last week, twenty minutes in, she saw his trainers pointing at the door, decided he wanted out, and ended early. That evening his dad phoned, annoyed. Oskar had loved the new song and lost forty minutes of his lesson.
examples.whatToDo: Note how Oskar sits when he arrives keen. Read a wish to leave only from a change, such as both hands dropping to his knees as he leans in.
examples.whyItMatters: The stool points his feet at the door every week. Only a change from his usual way of sitting tells Lucía he wants out.

questions.prompt: At the coffee machine, you tell a coworker about your weekend. She laughs at the funny part, but her feet have swung toward her desk. You launch into a second story. What most likely happens?
choices: She will feel left out unless you ask about her weekend.
She will settle in, since her laughing shows she is enjoying it.
She will cut you off soon, however warm her laugh sounds.
questions.explanation: Her feet have swung toward her desk, so part of her is already leaving, and the laugh is the polite face people learn to wear. Asking about her weekend fixes a problem she never showed.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "The client smiled all through my pitch, then put both hands on his knees and leaned forward. I think it went great." What do you say back?
choices: "Great, so call him today and ask him to sign the contract."
"Hands on both knees, leaning in, often means he was ready to finish."
"Leaning forward shows he was keen, so bring him even more detail next time."
questions.explanation: Both hands on the knees with the weight tipping forward is the knee clasp, a sign someone is ready to end the meeting. Asking for the contract today pushes a man who wanted to leave for a big yes.

questions.prompt: A vet is explaining a new feeding plan to a dog owner. He nods along, but his feet now point at the waiting-room door. She stops, prints the plan for him, and he thanks her warmly. Why did stopping help?
choices: His feet showed he wanted to go, though his nods said otherwise.
Owners take in feeding plans better on paper than when they hear them.
His nodding showed he had understood enough to need no more.
questions.explanation: His feet turned toward the door while his head kept nodding, and feet are the part people rarely learn to manage. The printout helped, but the real win was stopping when he wanted out.

questions.prompt: You're walking a colleague through a new shift rota. When you began, he stood facing you squarely. Halfway through, one of his feet has turned toward the lift. What should you do now?
choices: Keep going to the end, then ask if he has any questions.
Ask whether the new rota upsets him, since something changed.
Pause, give him the short version, and offer to finish later.
questions.explanation: He stood facing you at the start, so his foot turning toward the lift is a change, and it says he wants to go. Saving questions for the end keeps him there after he has stopped listening.

questions.prompt: Every evening your neighbour chats over the fence with her feet aimed at her back door, and stays for half an hour. Tonight she stands the same way, so you wish her goodnight after a minute. She looks hurt. What was the trap?
choices: Cutting her short without first asking how her day had gone.
Acting too slowly on what her feet were showing.
Reading her usual stance as a sudden wish to leave.
questions.explanation: Her feet pointed at her door every evening, and she still stayed half an hour. A turn only tells you something when it changes from how she usually stands. Acting faster would only have hurt her sooner.

questions.prompt: In a job interview, the manager smiles and says the candidate's answers are great. Then both her hands land on her knees and she leans forward. He starts a long story about his last job. What is she likely to do next?
choices: She cuts the story short and starts to wrap things up.
She leans further in, eager to hear more about his last job.
She lets him finish, then turns to her next question.
questions.explanation: Both hands on her knees with her weight tipping forward is the knee clasp, a sign she is ready to end the meeting. Here the lean is part of getting up to go, not a wish for more stories.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "My landlord smiles whenever I bring up the damp in my bathroom, but within a minute his feet swing toward his car. How do I get him to fix it?" What's the best advice to give?
choices: "Stop raising the damp with him, since his feet show he doesn't care."
"Keep it to one sentence, then ask when he has ten minutes."
"Explain the whole problem first, then check whether his feet turn."
questions.explanation: His feet swing toward his car, so he wants to leave even while he smiles. One sentence and a set time fit that. Explaining the whole problem first keeps him standing there, waiting to go.

When I say good morning to the first person I talk to each day, I glance at where their feet point, so I can spot it later if they turn away.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the day ends, watch one conversation you are not part of, at a shop counter or a bus stop, and notice whose feet turn away first.

chapters.title: When the Smile Says Yes and the Chest Turns Away
chapters.hook: One click from sending a rescue form, you hear your partner say a dog would be lovely. Their smile is warm; their chest swings away.
chapters.counterintuition: If someone smiles and chats with you, they must be enjoying it. It sounds right, and it fails for one reason: a smile is easy to put on out of kindness, while the chest turns before we think. Watch which way the chest points.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Notice which way someone's chest points; people turn toward those they like and away when uncomfortable.
chapters.tryThisNow: At dinner tonight, note which way the other person's chest points, then watch it again as you raise a harder topic.

memorableLines.text: A smile can be good manners, but the chest shows what someone welcomes.

breakdown.fastRead:
Hana is one click from sending the rescue centre's form for a scruffy terrier. Her partner, Rory, smiled and said a dog would be lovely, but his chest has just turned toward the TV. A minute ago, laughing about his football team, he sat turned fully toward her. Hana reads the smile as a yes. One click could bring home a dog only one of them wants.

A smile is easy to give out of kindness. Joe Navarro looks lower, at the chest. The old part of the brain, which reacts before we think, makes people lean toward what they like and away from what they don't. Pointing your chest at someone is what he calls ventral fronting, a sign of comfort. Turning it away is ventral denial, a sign of discomfort or dislike. The turn can be small. The change from a moment ago tells you most, often just as a hard topic comes up.

So when a chest swings away at one topic, ask about that topic. Hana takes her hand off the mouse and asks what part of a dog worries him. Rory turns back toward her and admits the early walks scare him. People turn their chests away from a topic that troubles them, and the turn tells more than the smile above it.

breakdown.fullRead:
Hana is one click from sending the rescue centre's form for a scruffy terrier. Her partner, Rory, smiled and said a dog would be lovely, but his chest has just turned toward the TV. It is Sunday evening, and the terrier's photo fills her laptop screen. A minute ago, laughing about his football team, Rory sat turned fully toward her, one knee up on the cushion. Hana reads the smile as a yes. One click could bring home a dog only one of them wants, and a dog is hard to send back.

Her reading makes sense. He smiled, he said yes, and he kept chatting. Most people take that as the whole answer. But from childhood we learn to smile to keep things pleasant, and to say yes when someone we love is excited. Rory does not want to spoil her evening. So the smile is real kindness, and it tells her almost nothing about the dog. If she sends the form, the doubt he swallowed tonight may come out later, on a cold, dark morning walk.

Joe Navarro looks below the face, at the chest. The limbic system is the old part of the brain that reacts before we think. It makes people lean toward what they like and away from what they don't, fast and without asking. That is why the body's lean is harder to manage than a smile. Pointing your chest and belly at someone is what he calls ventral fronting, and it shows comfort. Turning them away is ventral denial, and it shows discomfort or dislike. People do both all day without noticing, toward a friend across a room and away from a subject they would rather not touch.

The turn is often small. It may be a quarter turn, or one shoulder swinging back while the rest stays put. A small turn is easy to miss and easy to misread, so Navarro's method is to compare. First notice how the person sits while the talk is easy. That is their normal, the baseline you measure from. Then watch what happens when a harder topic comes up. The change from a moment ago tells you far more than any one way of sitting.

Context counts too. Someone who always sits at an angle, because of a stiff back or the shape of the sofa, is just sitting. Someone who turns to grab the remote is just grabbing the remote. The turn worth reading comes just as a topic arrives, and it stays. It says more when other signs join it at the same moment, like arms or a cushion pulled across the belly. One sign can be chance. Several together are hard to wave away.

Run that on Rory. While he talked football, he faced her fully. When she said dog, nothing changed on the TV, and the remote sat untouched on the table. Yet his chest swung toward the screen and stayed there, and he pulled a cushion onto his lap. The turn landed on one word. It is not about Hana, whom he faced happily a minute earlier. It is about the dog.

So when a chest swings away at one topic, slow down before you take the yes. Ask a gentle question about the topic itself. Then watch whether the chest comes back toward you.

Hana takes her hand off the mouse and asks what part of a dog worries him. Rory turns back toward her, drops the cushion, and admits the early walks before work scare him. Now they can plan the walks together, or look for a calmer dog, and the form can wait a day. People turn their chests away from a topic that troubles them, and the turn tells more than the smile above it.

examples.title: Splitting a cottage deposit on a park bench
examples.scenario: Zainab and her sister are on a park bench, planning a week in a seaside cottage. Her sister faced her the whole time, swapping ideas about beaches. When Zainab says the deposit is due Friday and they should split it, her sister smiles, says "Of course," and turns her chest toward the swings. Zainab's banking app is open, ready to pay it all.
examples.whatToDo: Hold off on paying. Ask her how the deposit sits with her budget this month, and watch whether she turns back.
examples.whyItMatters: Her chest turned at the money, not the trip, so asking now beats chasing half a deposit for weeks.

examples.title: Long division after a failed test
examples.scenario: Last month Callum asked his daughter Ivy if fractions made sense. She grinned, said yes, and he moved on. Her test came back with four marks out of twenty. Tonight, at the desk in her room, she faces him and chats about her friends. When he opens the long division sheet, she says, "Easy," and turns her chest toward the window.
examples.whatToDo: Treat her turn as the real answer. Work the first sum together, slowly, and ask which step feels hardest.
examples.whyItMatters: She faced him happily until the sheet came out, so the worry is about division, not about him.

examples.title: A new tablet with two minutes left
examples.scenario: Esther, a carer at a care home, has two minutes left on the morning medicine round. Mr Lindqvist usually faces her and asks about her garden. Today, when she says the doctor has added a new tablet, he smiles. "Whatever you say, love," he says, and turns his chest toward the window. In the next room a buzzer starts going, and Esther feels the minutes slip.
examples.whatToDo: Spend ten seconds asking gently what bothers him about the tablet, then pass his answer to the nurse.
examples.whyItMatters: His chest left her only when the tablet came up, and one question now may stop a quietly skipped dose.

questions.prompt: A friend pitched a new project to his manager over lunch. "She smiled and chatted the whole time, so she loves it," he tells you. What's your best reply?
choices: Did she stay facing you once you got to the details?
Did she smile with her eyes as well, or only with her mouth?
Then send her the full plan tonight while she's keen.
questions.explanation: Smiling and chatting are easy to give out of kindness. A change in how she sat once the details came up would show how the idea landed. Checking her eyes still only reads the smile.

questions.prompt: A wedding photographer shows a couple two packages. As she names the price of the bigger one, the groom smiles but turns his chest toward the window. She stops and asks what worries them about the cost, and they book the smaller package that day. Why did stopping work?
choices: The pause left a quiet gap, and the couple soon filled it with the truth.
His chest turned away at the price, which showed her where the worry was.
His turn showed he'd taken against her, so a softer touch was needed.
questions.explanation: His chest turned right as the price came up, so she knew the cost was the worry and asked about it. Nothing points to him disliking her, since the turn landed on the price.

questions.prompt: Your teenage son sits facing you at the kitchen counter, chatting about a game he's playing. You ask him to cook dinner every Thursday. He smiles, says "Okay," and turns his chest toward the hallway. What do you do?
choices: Explain why his help at home matters so much to you.
Wrap things up fast, since he clearly wants to get back upstairs.
Ask him gently what about cooking on Thursdays doesn't sit right.
questions.explanation: He faced you happily until the cooking came up, then turned away, so the worry is about cooking on Thursdays. Ask about that. Explaining why it matters talks past whatever is bothering him.

questions.prompt: A coworker agreed to help run the team's charity quiz night. At lunch she chatted and laughed with you, but when you said she'd handle the ticket money, she smiled and turned her chest toward the window. A week later she drops out. What was the trap?
choices: Taking her friendly chat as a yes to the money part too.
Not getting her to sign up in writing that same day.
Asking someone who doesn't much enjoy quiz nights to help you run one.
questions.explanation: Her chest turned away right as the ticket money came up, while the warm chat went on. That turn was her real answer to the money part. A written sign-up would only have locked in a doubtful yes.

questions.prompt: Your uncle always sits half-turned toward the window at family lunches. Today he sits the same way, smiling, while you tell him about your new job. If you ask how he really feels about it, what will you most likely hear?
choices: That he has doubts, since his chest is turned away from you.
That he's only being polite, since a smile is easy to fake.
That he's pleased, since that's how he always sits at lunch.
questions.explanation: What tells most is a change from how someone sat a moment ago. Your uncle sits this way at every lunch, and nothing shifted at your news. Reading doubt into his usual pose sees a turn that never happened, and with no turn, nothing hints his smile is mere manners.

questions.prompt: A colleague tells you, "When I mentioned the deadline, my client smiled but swung her chest away. Should I tell her I saw her turn away?" How do you answer?
choices: Yes, telling her shows that you're paying close attention to her.
Ask her about the deadline instead, and see if she turns back.
Drop the deadline for now, since raising it again would only annoy her.
questions.explanation: Her chest turned at the deadline, so that is the topic to ask about, gently. Pointing out her turn can feel like being caught. Once the worry is out, her chest often turns back toward your colleague.

questions.prompt: A swimming coach gives feedback to a swimmer who usually faces her and jokes back. When she mentions the relay, he says, "Fine, coach," and turns his chest toward the pool. After practice she asks him about the relay, and he opens up. What made his turn more useful than his words?
choices: His face would have shown it too, if she'd looked closer.
His turning away showed he dislikes her, so his 'fine' was a cover.
He turned right as the relay came up, showing what bothered him.
questions.explanation: He faced her and joked until the relay came up, then turned toward the pool. That change showed what bothered him. It can't be dislike of her, since he faced her happily a moment before.

reviewCards.front: A man asks his housemate to share the cost of a cleaner. She smiles, says "No problem," and turns her chest toward the window as he names the price. He books the cleaner, and three weeks later she still hasn't paid. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: He took her smile and her easy yes as the answer. Her chest turned away right at the price, and one gentle question about the cost then would have saved weeks of chasing.

reviewCards.front: In your own words: when someone smiles and agrees with you, what should you watch, and why?
reviewCards.back: Which way their chest points, and whether it turns away when a topic comes up. People turn toward what they're comfortable with and away from what bothers them, even while they smile.

reviewCards.front: You tell your sister you plan to move abroad. A minute ago she faced you, but now she says "Wow, exciting," and swings her chest toward the kitchen. What do you do?
reviewCards.back: Pause the plans and ask her gently how she really feels about you going. Her chest turned at the news, so the smile may not be the whole answer.

reviewCards.front: Your colleague sits turned toward the window in every meeting, even the cheerful ones. Why not read that as dislike?
reviewCards.back: Because that's how she always sits. What tells you something is a turn away from how she sat a moment before, often just as a hard topic comes up.

reviewCards.front: When someone smiles and says yes, but their chest turns away just as the topic comes up, the smile is ...
reviewCards.back: ... only part of the answer. The turn shows the topic bothers them, so ask about it gently before taking the yes.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Spotting the moment someone's upper body swings away from you mid-talk, and checking in before you count on their yes.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I sit down across from someone to talk something through, I notice which way their chest points while the talk is still easy.
When I catch myself thinking, "They smiled, so they're fine with it", I recall which way their chest turned at that moment, and ask again gently if it turned away.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In one talk today, notice how the other person sits at the start. When you reach a trickier subject, check whether their chest turns away, and if it does, ask one gentle question about that subject.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a day this week, pick one chat at home or at work. Notice where the other person's chest points early on, and again when something tricky comes up. Jot down any turn you see and what it turned out to mean.

chapters.title: When Busy Arms Go Still, Look for the Worry
chapters.hook: Ask your friend about her weekend, and her arms fly. Ask about the money she owes you, and they drop stiff to her sides.
chapters.counterintuition: The usual advice is to read faces and words, since arms only carry things. Watching for arms that suddenly go still works better, because fear freezes the body before we think, and the arms show it plainly.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When someone's arms suddenly go still or pull in tight, look for fear, shame, or something held back.
chapters.tryThisNow: Notice, in your next conversation today, how much the other person's arms move while the talk feels easy.

memorableLines.text: Busy arms that suddenly go still are holding back a worry.

breakdown.fastRead:
Joel, the new apprentice at Adaeze's bike repair shop, talks with both arms, waving a spoke wrench as he explains a wheel. Then Adaeze asks about a customer's racing bike, due back at five, and his arms drop to his sides. He says it's fine. What just happened?

Joe Navarro's answer is that arms tell the truth about our feelings. The limbic system, the brain's alarm that reacts before we think, freezes us when it senses a threat. The arms go still or tuck in tight. People hold their arms back when they are afraid, scolded or hiding something. What counts is the change from a person's baseline, the way they move when calm.

Adaeze knows Joel's baseline, and the stillness came with one question, not a cold draught. It tells her a worry sits behind that bike, though not which worry. Once the shop is empty, she asks again, quietly and without blame. He admits he scratched the frame and was scared to say, so she calls the owner before five. Think arms are just for carrying, and you would believe him when he says it's fine and meet an angry customer at pickup. When someone's busy arms suddenly go still or pull in tight, ask gently about what just came up; the arms have told you something is wrong, and a calm question may let the person say what.

Then Adaeze asks about a customer's racing bike, due back to its owner at five, and his arms drop to his sides. He says it's fine and goes quiet. Adaeze has a small shop and a loyal customer who rides that bike every weekend. What just happened?

Joe Navarro's answer is that arms tell the truth about our feelings. The limbic system, the brain's alarm that reacts before we think, freezes us when it senses a threat. Long ago, staying still kept people from being noticed by danger, and the arms still obey. They go still or tuck in tight. Navarro sees this when people are afraid, when they are being scolded, and when they are hiding something. Picture a child being told off, standing stiff with arms pinned to the sides. What counts is the change from a person's baseline, the way that person moves when calm.

Adaeze has watched Joel for weeks, so she knows his baseline. His arms never rest. This time they stopped on one question, not in a cold draught or at the end of a long day. That tells her a worry sits behind the racing bike, though not which worry. It is no proof of a lie. So she waits until the shop is empty and asks again, quietly and without blame. Joel admits he slipped with a wrench and scratched the frame. He was scared to say. Adaeze calls the owner before five and offers to fix the paint at no charge. As Joel talks, his hands start moving again.

Most people think arms are just for carrying things. They watch the face, take the easy words and move on. Adaeze would then have heard that all was fine and met an angry customer at the counter, with no warning and no plan. The arms had answered her question before Joel did. When someone's busy arms suddenly go still or pull in tight, ask gently about what just came up; the arms have told you something is wrong, and a calm question may let the person say what.
breakdown.fullRead:
Joel, the new apprentice at Adaeze's bike repair shop, talks with both arms, waving a spoke wrench as he explains a wheel. Then Adaeze asks about a customer's racing bike, due back to its owner at five, and his arms drop to his sides. He says it's fine and goes quiet. Adaeze has a small shop and a loyal customer who rides that bike every weekend. What just happened, and should she care?

Joe Navarro's answer is that arms tell the truth about our feelings. The limbic system, the brain's alarm that reacts before we think, freezes us when it senses a threat. Long ago, staying still kept people from being noticed by whatever hunted them. The habit never left. When something feels dangerous, even a question, the arms go still or tuck in tight. Often this happens before the person even knows they are worried.

Arms show good feelings just as honestly. Navarro calls arms thrown up high at good news gravity-defying, because joy lifts them against their own weight. Think of fans flinging their arms up when their team scores. Fear, shame and secrets do the opposite. They pull the arms down and in, or hold them still, as if the body wants to take up less room.

Navarro sees this holding back in three moments above all. People restrict their arms when they are afraid, when they are being scolded, and when they are hiding something. Picture a child being told off, standing stiff with arms pinned to the sides. The child is not choosing that pose. The feeling brain chose it first.

None of this means much without a baseline, which is the way a person moves when calm. A naturally quiet man who keeps his arms still is only being himself. What counts is a change from that person's usual way of moving, and the moment it happens. Arms that stop at one question say more than arms that are still all day. Navarro also asks you to read the scene around the change. A cold draught or the end of a long shift can still the arms too. Other signs at the same moment, such as a voice that drops, make the reading stronger.

Adaeze has watched Joel for weeks, so she knows his baseline. His arms never rest. This time they stopped on one question, in a warm shop at ten in the morning, and his voice went flat as well. That tells her a worry sits behind the racing bike, though not which worry. It is no proof of a lie. So she waits until the shop is empty and asks again, quietly and without blame. Joel admits he slipped with a wrench and scratched the frame. He was scared to say. Adaeze calls the owner before five and offers to fix the paint at no charge. As Joel talks it through, his hands start moving again.

Most people think arms are just for carrying things. They watch the face, take the easy words and move on. Adaeze would then have heard that all was fine and met an angry customer at the counter, with no warning and no plan. Getting cross would have failed too. Since scolding is one of the things that pins arms down, it would likely have made Joel freeze harder. The arms had answered her question before Joel did, and she only had to ask in a way that let him catch up. When someone's busy arms suddenly go still or pull in tight, ask gently about what just came up; the arms have told you something is wrong, and a calm question may let the person say what.

examples.title: The backup nobody mentioned
examples.scenario: Sanne, a freelance editor, cuts wedding films in the back bedroom she uses as a studio. Her part-time assistant, Rashid, explains every cut with both hands. Today she asks whether he backed up the couple's footage last night. His arms drop and his hands stay pinned in his lap. "Should be done," he says. The couple collects their film on Friday, and Sanne feels a flicker of doubt.
examples.whatToDo: Read the still arms as a worry about the backup. Ask him calmly what happened last night, then check the drive together.
examples.whyItMatters: If footage is missing, she finds out today, with time to recover it before the couple's Friday pickup.

examples.title: Ten days until the bookkeeping exam
examples.scenario: Ibrahim sits beside his study partner, Delphine, in an evening bookkeeping class. She usually waves her pencil while she talks through each sum. Last week the tutor asked who had finished the practice test, and her arms pulled tight to her sides. Ibrahim took her "all done" at face value. This week her chair is empty, and the exam is ten days away.
examples.whatToDo: Message her that you noticed she went quiet when the practice test came up, and offer to work through it together.
examples.whyItMatters: A worry noticed early, and met kindly, gives her a reason to come back before the exam.

examples.title: Who shrank the wool jumper?
examples.scenario: Teodor pulls his favourite wool jumper out of the washing machine, shrunk to fit a child. His daughter, Mirela, did the laundry this week. She usually swings her arms when she talks, but now she stands in the doorway with them pinned stiff at her sides. Teodor feels his face go hot. "Who put this on a hot wash?" he snaps.
examples.whatToDo: Put the jumper down, lower your voice and tell her you are not angry with her. Then ask gently what happened with the wash.
examples.whyItMatters: Her pinned arms already show fear. A snap would freeze her tighter, while a calm question lets her own the mistake.

questions.prompt: Before each lesson, a driving instructor's learner chats in the parked car with both hands flying. Today she asks whether he practised parallel parking, and his arms pull tight to his sides. Why is that change worth noticing?
choices: Still arms show he is lying, so she can catch the fib early.
His arms usually fly, so stopping at that question points to a hidden worry.
Tight arms show he is tired, so a shorter lesson today would suit him better.
questions.explanation: His arms moved freely until that one question, so the question touched a worry. Stillness points to a feeling, not a lie, and it came with the question rather than with tiredness.

questions.prompt: Your housemate tells every story with both arms. On the sofa you ask whether the rent transfer went through. "All sorted," they say, arms pulled in tight around a mug. What is your next move?
choices: Remind them firmly that rent is due Friday and the landlord won't wait.
Accept their "all sorted" as the full answer, and go back to watching the film together.
Say gently that if the transfer hit a snag, you can sort it out together.
questions.explanation: Their arms pulled in at the rent question, so a worry likely sits behind their easy answer. A gentle offer lets it out. A firm reminder works like scolding, which only holds the arms tighter.

questions.prompt: A new cashier at a garden centre has stood with her arms close and still since her first shift. When the till comes up short, her supervisor decides those still arms point to her. What is the trap?
choices: Judging stillness that has been her normal way of standing since day one.
Studying her arms, when her face would show any guilt more clearly.
Watching her arms on busy shifts instead of in calm moments at the till.
questions.explanation: Her arms have been still since her first shift, so stillness is simply how she stands. Only a change from someone's usual way of moving tells you something, busy shift or calm.

questions.prompt: A choir singer who usually conducts along with both hands goes still, hugging her music folder, when the leader mentions next month's solo. After rehearsal, the leader asks her quietly, without blame, how she feels about it. What does asking this way give the best chance of?
choices: She says she is fine, and the leader learns nothing more about it.
She admits the solo scares her, and they plan a few extra run-throughs together.
She feels relieved to hear the solo can go to a singer who wants it more.
questions.explanation: Her arms froze at the solo, a sign of worry. A quiet question without blame, away from the group, gives that worry room to come out. Handing the solo away settles nothing, since nobody learns what the worry was.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "My brother always talks with his hands. When I asked about his new job, his arms went stiff at his sides. But he said it's great, so it's great." What is your best reply?
choices: His arms stopped right at the job question, so ask him again, alone and gently.
Stiff arms like that usually mean he was cold or worn out, so let it go.
Watch his face next time instead, since a face shows what he really feels.
questions.explanation: He usually talks with his hands, so stiff arms at the job question show a worry behind it. Asking again, alone and gently, gives it room. Nothing points to a chill; the change came with one question.

questions.prompt: At an adult swimming class, a learner who chats with big arm sweeps goes still, arms pressed to her ribs, when the coach mentions the deep end. "I'm ready," she says. Why should the coach trust her arms over her words?
choices: Arms are harder to fake than faces, so her words are a lie.
She is choosing to hold her arms back to hide her fear from the class.
Fear freezes the body before we can think, and her arms usually sweep wide.
questions.explanation: Her arms sweep when she is at ease and froze at the deep end, a change made before she could think. That is why it beats her words, and why it signals fear rather than a lie.

questions.prompt: At a community garden, a volunteer who waves both arms while he chats goes still, hands pinned to his sides, when someone mentions the broken shed lock. What should you do about it?
choices: Find a quiet moment later and ask him how the shed has been going.
Ask him in front of the group why his arms went so stiff just then.
Change the subject quickly so he does not feel put on the spot.
questions.explanation: His arms froze at the lock, so a worry sits there. A private, gentle question lets him say it. Naming his stiff arms in front of the group feels like a scolding and freezes him further.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what should you do when someone's lively arms suddenly go still or tuck in close?
reviewCards.back: Take it as a sign of fear, shame or a worry they are holding back, and gently ask about whatever just came up.

reviewCards.front: Your teenager usually flings his arms around while talking, but goes stiff-armed when you ask how the maths test went.
reviewCards.back: Read the stillness as a worry about the test. Later, alone and calmly, ask how it really went, without any blame.

reviewCards.front: Why can a sudden stop in someone's arm movement tell you more than their words?
reviewCards.back: The feeling brain freezes the body at a threat before we think, so the arms show worry even while the words say all is fine.

reviewCards.front: Still arms only tell you something when you already know ...
reviewCards.back: ... how that person usually moves when calm, so you can see the change and the moment it came.

reviewCards.front: A manager saw a quiet new hire keep her arms still in every meeting and decided she was hiding problems with her work. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: The manager never learned how she usually moves. Her arms were always still, so there was no change to read and nothing to conclude.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Spotting the moment someone's arms stop moving, and asking kindly about what caused it.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I ask someone at home how their day went, I watch their arms as they answer and note how much they move when relaxed.
When I notice I accepted someone's "fine" while their arms had gone still, I go back to them alone and gently ask about that topic again.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the day ends, ask someone a question you suspect is a sore point, and watch whether their arms move less than before. If they do, follow up with a softer question.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each evening this week, pick one person you talked with and recall how their arms moved at the start and at any hard topic. Note any change, and what came out when you asked.

chapters.title: Why Hidden Hands Cost You Trust
chapters.hook: You're explaining your plan across the table, every word true, and your hands rest in your lap. The people listening already trust you less.
chapters.counterintuition: We tend to think only our words count, so where our hands rest doesn't matter. What works is keeping your hands where people can see them, since listeners grow wary of hands they can't see, even when you have nothing to hide.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Keep your hands where people can see them while you talk, because hidden hands make listeners trust you less.
chapters.tryThisNow: Move the clutter off the front edge of your desk or table today, and rest both hands there while you talk.

memorableLines.text: Honest words land better when the listener can see the hands that go with them.

breakdown.fastRead:
Where your hands are can decide whether your honest words get believed. Joe Navarro says people grow wary of anyone who talks with hidden hands, tucked under a table or deep in a pocket. Listeners sense something is being held back, even when nothing is.

Picture Elif at the bank on a Tuesday morning, asking for a loan to open her flower stall. Every number she gives is true. But her hands sit clasped in her lap, below the edge of the desk. The adviser leans back and asks for the same figures again. She could lose the loan without one false word. Most of us would sit the same way. We learn early that words are what get judged, and while we talk we cannot see our own hands.

The fix comes before the first word. Rest your hands on the desk or table, where the other person can see them. Keep them there through the hard questions, not only the easy start. If you are standing, keep them out of your pockets. Elif lays her hands beside her papers and runs a finger along each figure as she explains it. Now her hands back up her words. Keep your hands in plain sight whenever you talk, and your honest words will be easier to trust.

Listeners sense something is being held back, even when nothing is. The words can be true from start to finish, and the doubt still creeps in.

His advice follows from that. In talks, interviews and meetings, keep your hands up and visible. Then they back up what you say instead of raising questions about it. Hands go missing in a few easy ways. They slide off the table into a lap, they rest under a bag, or they disappear into pockets. Each one leaves the listener facing a person with part of the picture gone.

Picture Elif at the bank on a Tuesday morning, asking for a loan to open her flower stall. She has practised her figures for a week, and every number she gives is true. But her hands sit clasped in her lap, below the edge of the desk. The adviser leans back and asks for the same figures again, then asks how sure she is about the rent. She could lose the loan without one false word.

Nothing Elif says is wrong, so she hunts for the problem in her words. Maybe the rent figure sounded too low. Maybe she spoke too fast. She starts to explain everything twice, and the meeting grows longer and stiffer. The trouble was never in her sentences. The adviser could hear every one of them but could not see her hands.

Most of us would sit the same way. We learn early that words are what get judged, so we polish them and forget the rest. While we talk we cannot see our own hands, so we lose track of them. Tucking them away can even feel calm and polite, a way to keep still and not fuss. The listener sees what we miss, a person whose hands have gone out of sight.

The fix comes before the first word. When you sit down, move any bag, coat or folder off your lap. Rest your hands on the desk or table, where the other person can see them. They do not need to do anything clever. Open and resting is enough, and they can move a little as you explain.

Then keep them there through the hard questions too. Those are the answers you most need believed, so they are the worst moment for your hands to vanish. If you are standing, keep your hands out of your pockets and in front of you. The same goes at home. Telling your brother why you can't lend him the car this weekend, with your hands jammed in your coat pockets, invites the same quiet doubt as the desk at the bank.

Elif tries again with the next question. She lays her hands beside her papers and runs a finger along each figure as she explains it. The adviser stops leaning back and starts writing the numbers down. Her figures are the same as before, but now her hands back them up. Keep your hands in plain sight whenever you talk, and your honest words will be easier to trust.

examples.title: Breaking news of weekend shifts on the sofa
examples.scenario: Bongani has to tell his partner, Irene, that he has agreed to three months of Saturday shifts. It really does end in March, and he needs her to believe that. They sit at opposite ends of the sofa after dinner, the TV on mute. His hands are pushed deep into the front pocket of his hoodie. He takes a breath to begin.
examples.whatToDo: Pull your hands out of the hoodie, rest them on the cushion between you, then explain the shifts and the March end date.
examples.whyItMatters: With his hands in sight, Irene hears the March promise without sensing anything held back, so it sounds as true as it is.

examples.title: The late van and the rehearsed account
examples.scenario: Teodora runs the early shift at a parcel depot. Yesterday a van left forty minutes late, so she rehearsed her account all evening and printed a timeline. Now she stands at the manager's desk with both hands in her fleece pockets, every word ready. She needs the manager to believe her account the first time.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the timeline, but lay it on the desk with both hands beside it and walk the manager through each step.
examples.whyItMatters: Her careful words are not the problem. With her hands out of her pockets, they back her account up instead of raising doubt.

examples.title: Defending an essay mark to a tutor
examples.scenario: Sachin books a meeting with his university tutor to ask for a second look at his history essay mark. He knows his sources are solid. Within a minute she pushes back and says section two never proves its point. His face goes hot, and his hands slide off the table into his lap. She turns the essay toward him and says, "Show me where."
examples.whatToDo: Bring your hands back onto the table, put a finger on the paragraph she means, and walk her through the source that proves it.
examples.whyItMatters: She already doubts the essay. Hands back in sight keep his true answer from looking like a dodge while he makes his case.

questions.prompt: You sit down with your gym's manager to explain why you need to pause your membership. Every reason you'll give is true. Your bag is on your lap, and your hands rest on it below the table. What do you do?
choices: Leave your hands resting on the bag and choose every word with great care.
Bring your hands up once the manager starts asking you questions.
Put the bag on the floor and rest your hands on the table.
questions.explanation: With the bag on the floor and your hands on the table, the manager sees them from your first true word. Waiting for questions means your whole opening is heard with your hands out of sight.

questions.prompt: A plumber explains a big repair bill at a homeowner's front door, smiling, with both hands in his jacket pockets. Every figure he gives is true. She asks for a second quote anyway. What tripped him up?
choices: Believing true figures speak for themselves, wherever his hands are.
Believing a warm smile would make a big bill easier to accept.
Believing the homeowner needed every single cost spelled out.
questions.explanation: His figures were true, but with his hands hidden she sensed something held back. The smile was never the problem. The doubt came from the hands she could not see.

questions.prompt: A car seller rests her hands on the desk while she praises a used car. When the buyer asks about past accidents, she drops her hands into her lap to answer. What is most likely to happen next?
choices: The buyer trusts her more for staying calm on a hard question.
The buyer starts to doubt the answer about past accidents.
The buyer notices nothing, since her words sound sure.
questions.explanation: Her hands went out of sight right at the hardest question, so the buyer senses something held back there. Confident words cannot make up for hands the buyer can no longer see.

questions.prompt: A friend is about to ask her boss for a raise. She says, "I'll sit back with my hands in my lap, so I look relaxed and not pushy." What's the best thing to tell her?
choices: Sit up straight and hold eye contact so you look confident.
Stay relaxed at first, and show your hands at the end.
Rest your hands on the desk, where your boss can see them.
questions.explanation: A boss who can see her hands has nothing to wonder about while she makes her case. Eye contact helps, but her hands would still be hidden in her lap. Showing them only at the end leaves most of her case heard with hidden hands.

questions.prompt: A financial adviser clears her desk before each meeting and keeps her hands resting on it while she talks. Her clients often say they trust her. Why does this help?
choices: Hands on the desk make her look calmer than she feels.
Clients can see her hands, so nothing seems held back.
A clear desk shows clients she is well organised.
questions.explanation: When listeners cannot see a speaker's hands, they sense something held back. Her hands on the desk remove that doubt. A tidy desk may look good, but the trust comes from hands they can see.

questions.prompt: You're giving a five-minute talk at your library's open evening, standing with no table in front of you. Halfway through, your hands keep drifting toward your pockets. What's your move?
choices: Keep them out of your pockets and in front of you.
Clasp them behind your back so they stay out of the way.
Watch the audience's hands to see if they relax.
questions.explanation: Out of your pockets and in front of you, your hands stay where the room can see them. Clasped behind your back, your hands are just as hidden as they are in your pockets.

questions.prompt: A wedding planner meets a couple with her hands open on the table. When they ask about extra fees, she slides her hands under the thick folder on her lap. They book a different planner. What trap did she fall into?
choices: Thinking the couple only wanted a cheaper planner anyway.
Thinking open hands at the start would cover the whole meeting.
Thinking a thick folder full of prices would make her look prepared.
questions.explanation: Her hands vanished just as the couple asked about fees, so that answer felt held back. Open hands earlier did not carry over. The folder was fine, but hiding her hands under it was not.

reviewCards.front: You're about to explain a billing mistake to a client across a small meeting table, and your hands are folded in your lap.
reviewCards.back: Bring your hands up and rest them on the table before you start, so the client can see them while you explain.

reviewCards.front: Why might a listener doubt an honest answer when the speaker's hands are under the table?
reviewCards.back: When hands are out of sight, listeners sense something is being held back, even when nothing is, so they trust the words less.
