reviewCards.back: ... rest them on the desk or table in plain sight, so they back up your words from the very start.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what should you do with your hands when you talk, and why?
reviewCards.back: Keep them where people can see them, because hidden hands make listeners trust you less, even when every word is true.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Letting people see your hands while you speak, so nothing about you seems held back.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I catch myself rehearsing what to say before a serious talk, I also check my hands and bring them out of my lap or pockets.
When I sit down across a desk or table to talk, I move any bag or coat off my lap and rest my hands on the table.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before you go to bed tonight, have one sit-down talk with both hands resting on the table the whole time, and notice when they try to slip away.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each time you sit down for a meeting or a serious talk this week, check your hands in the first minute. If they're in your lap or pockets, bring them up where the other person can see them.

chapters.title: When the Eyes Narrow at One Name
chapters.hook: A friend can agree to every name you read out. Their eyes may still narrow at one, and that narrowing is the real answer.
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think you can't know how someone feels about a name until they say so. Actually, their eyes often tell you first, because the brain narrows them on its own to shut out something it does not want to hear.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When someone's eyes narrow or squint at one name or word, that word bothers them.
chapters.tryThisNow: Ask one person you see today about three people you both know, naming them one at a time while you watch their eyes.

memorableLines.text: Eyes that tighten at one name tell you what a polite yes hides.

breakdown.fastRead:
Kenji is reading the guest list for his mother's sixtieth birthday aloud. His wife, Aroha, says yes to every name, but at his cousin Mele's, her eyes narrow for a blink before she nods. Kenji is ready to send the invites, since nobody objected. If that name is a sore spot, the party could turn cold across the cake.

But a yes is easy to fake. Joe Navarro watches the eyes instead. When we hear something unwelcome, the brain tries to shut it out, so the eyes narrow, squint or close for a moment. He calls this eye blocking. Investigators once faced a spy who was cooperating but would not name the people who had helped him. They showed him 32 cards, each with one name. At two names his pupils shrank and he squinted a little. The two people named later confessed.

The narrowing lasts only a moment, so watch as each name lands. Kenji reads the list again, slowly, with his eyes on hers. The squint comes at Mele and nowhere else. He gently asks whether something happened with Mele. Aroha admits they fell out last spring, and Kenji seats them at opposite ends of the table. Once you watch the eyes as each name is said, you see which one bothers someone before they speak.

Many of us think we cannot know how someone feels about a person until they tell us. But words are the easiest thing to manage. Joe Navarro adds that the face is the part of the body people most learn to control. Most of us learned as children to smile at a gift we did not like. So a nod tells Kenji very little.

The eyes are harder to manage. Navarro traces this to the limbic brain, the old part of the brain that reacts before we have time to think. When we see or hear something unwelcome, it tries to block it out. The eyes narrow, squint or close for a moment. Sometimes a hand comes up to cover them. He calls this eye blocking. Even the pupils, the black centres of the eyes, can shrink.

Investigators once leaned on exactly this. A spy who was cooperating with them still would not name the people who had helped him. So they showed him 32 cards, each with one name on it. At two of the names, his pupils got smaller and he squinted a little. He had named no one, yet his eyes had picked out two. The two people on those cards later confessed.

The cards worked because of how they were built. Each one held a single name, so each reaction could only belong to that name. The other names passed without the squint. Two did not. That difference, at one name and not the rest, is what made the signal worth trusting. Nobody had to argue with the spy or catch him out. They only had to watch his eyes as each name came up.

You can run the same check at home or at work. Say names one at a time, with a small pause after each, and keep your eyes on the other person's. The narrowing lasts only a moment, so watch as each word lands, not at the end. Look for a squint at one name only. If the sun is in their face and they squint at everything, it means nothing. It helps when something else agrees, such as lips pressed tight at the same moment.

Then be clear about what you have learned. A squint tells you a word bothers someone. It does not tell you why, and it is not proof of a lie. So the next step is a gentle question about that one name or word. It works with more than names, too. A day of the week, a task, a place or a plan can draw the same quick narrowing.

Kenji reads the list again, slowly, with his eyes on hers. The squint comes at Mele and nowhere else. He gently asks whether something happened with Mele. Aroha admits they fell out last spring, and Kenji seats them at opposite ends of the table. The cake gets cut in peace. Once you watch the eyes as each name is said, you see which one bothers someone before they speak.

examples.title: Honey jars for a new deli
examples.scenario: Farida sells honey from a weekend market stall, and a deli owner has finally agreed to stock six jars. Farida offers to put them by the till, in the window, or beside the jam from Hollow Farm. At the farm's name, the owner's eyes narrow for a blink. "Anywhere's fine," she says. Farida stands holding the crate, deciding.
examples.whatToDo: Put the jars by the till, away from the farm's jam, and later ask lightly how the deli gets on with that farm.
examples.whyItMatters: The owner's eyes tightened at one name only, so the honey starts life far from whatever bothers her.

examples.title: A recovery plan he said yes to
examples.scenario: After her dad's hip operation, Imani read him his recovery plan: daily walks, stretches, and twice-weekly pool sessions. His eyes narrowed at "pool," but he said yes to everything, so she booked it. Three weeks later he has walked every day and skipped every swim. His physio says the hip is getting stiff.
examples.whatToDo: Go back to the pool on its own and gently ask him what makes it hard, before booking any more sessions.
examples.whyItMatters: His eyes had already marked the one part that bothered him, and his yes kept the real problem hidden.

examples.title: Five names said in one breath
examples.scenario: Luka, fifteen, captains his school's debate club and must find his friend Noor a partner for Friday's practice round. At lunch he read her the five possible partners in one quick breath, watching her eyes. They narrowed somewhere in the middle. She shrugged and said, "Whoever." Now he can't tell which name did it.
examples.whatToDo: Read the names again, one at a time with a short pause after each, and quietly ask about the one her eyes tighten at.
examples.whyItMatters: A pause gives each name its own moment, so the squint points to one partner and Noor isn't stuck with them.

questions.prompt: You read your brother three towns for the family's summer week. At the second, his eyes narrow for a moment, then he says, "All fine." You book it, and he sulks all week. What was the trap?
choices: Taking his "all fine" as the answer when his eyes narrowed at that town.
Booking before you asked the rest of the family which town they liked.
Saying the towns out loud instead of sending him a list to read alone later.
questions.explanation: His eyes narrowed at that one town before his words smoothed it over, so the narrowing was the real answer. A list read alone would have hidden that signal from you.

questions.prompt: A cinema manager reads a new usher the open shifts, one day at a time. At "Sunday" her eyes squint, though she says any day works. He asks softly, "Is Sunday a hard one?" What most likely happens next?
choices: She feels watched too closely and starts to doubt the new job.
She repeats that any day works, since she already said so to him earlier.
She explains what makes Sundays hard, and the schedule is built around it.
questions.explanation: His soft question is about the one day her eyes reacted to, which gives her room to say what is wrong. Nothing in it asks her to defend her earlier answer, so she has no reason to repeat it.

questions.prompt: A friend who runs a small office says, "I'll ask the new hire which coworker she'd like to shadow. If she minds anyone, she'll tell me." What is your best reply?
choices: "Say the names one at a time and notice which one makes her eyes tighten."
"Wait until she has settled in for a few weeks and feels safe enough to speak."
"Send her the names by email so she can answer honestly without being watched."
questions.explanation: A new hire may say she minds no one, but her eyes can narrow at a name before she speaks. An email strips away that signal and leaves only her polite answer.

questions.prompt: A pharmacist goes through an older man's medicines aloud, one name at a time. At one pill's name, his eyes narrow. She asks about it, and he admits it upsets his stomach. Why did watching his eyes help?
choices: The slow pace calmed him enough to finally mention the stomach trouble.
Hearing each name out loud jogged his memory about which of his pills was the problem.
His eyes narrowed by themselves at that pill, before he had picked his words.
questions.explanation: His eyes narrowed on their own the moment he heard that name, before he decided what to say. That pointed her to the one pill to ask about. A slow pace alone could not have done that.

questions.prompt: On a video call, a client agrees to your kitchen redesign. When you mention the electrician you plan to use, his eyes squint, then he says, "Great." What is your next move?
choices: Carry on as planned, since he said great and seemed happy.
Ask him lightly how he feels about that electrician before booking anyone.
Quietly book a different electrician, since the squint shows he dislikes him.
questions.explanation: The squint came at the electrician, not at the design, so that one name is what bothers him. Asking lightly before you book lets him say why. Swapping electricians assumes a reason the squint never gave, and carrying on trusts his "great" over his eyes.

questions.prompt: A father asks his daughter which friend's house she was at, naming three girls. At one name she squints. He snaps, "So you're lying to me." She storms upstairs. Where did he go wrong?
choices: Listing names for her instead of letting her tell the whole story first.
Treating the squint as a lie, when it only showed that name bothered her.
Asking in such a sharp voice that she felt cornered right from the very start.
questions.explanation: The squint showed that one friend's name bothers her. It did not show why, and it did not prove a lie. Calling it one turned a clue that needed a gentle question into a fight.

questions.prompt: A mother reads her son the summer camps on offer, glancing at her notes as she goes. She looks up at the end to check his face. What will she most likely see?
choices: Little of use, since any squint came and went as each camp was named.
His real favorite, since his face settles on the camp he wants by the end.
A squint aimed at the camp he dislikes, held until she looks up.
questions.explanation: The narrowing lasts only a moment, right as each word lands. Looking up at the end misses it, so she needed to watch as each camp was named.

reviewCards.front: Why watch someone's eyes as you say each name, instead of trusting the yes they give at the end?
reviewCards.back: The eyes can narrow at a name that bothers them before they choose their words, and a polite yes can cover that up.

reviewCards.front: You read someone a list, and their eyes narrow at one item but not the others. That item ...
reviewCards.back: ... is the one that bothers them, so it's the one to ask about gently.

reviewCards.front: A drama club leader saw a member's eyes narrow at the word "lead" and told the group, "So you don't want the part." The member went quiet. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: The squint showed the word bothered them, not why. A quiet question could have found out whether it was nerves, a rival or something else before the part was given away.

reviewCards.front: In your own words: what does a squint at one name tell you, and what comes next?
reviewCards.back: That name bothers the person, whatever they say out loud. Next comes a gentle question about that one name.

reviewCards.front: You and your partner are picking a babysitter. You read three names from the neighborhood group, and at the second, your partner's eyes tighten for a moment.
reviewCards.back: Before booking anyone, quietly ask whether something about that name bothers them, and hear what your partner has to say.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Catching the quick tightening of the eyes that marks which name or word unsettles someone, then asking about it.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I realize I talked right past someone's squint at a name, I go back to that name and gently ask how they feel about it.
When I go over plans with someone at the start of the week, I name each person or place one at a time and watch their eyes as each lands.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one shared choice today, such as where to eat or which film to watch. Say each option on its own, watch the other person's eyes, and gently ask about any option that tightens them.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, when you hand out tasks or plan an outing with others, slow down at each name. Afterward, jot down any squint you saw and what you learned when you asked about it.

chapters.title: Treat Nervous Answers as a Flag, Not Proof
chapters.hook: A cracked tablet, and a son who rubs his palms and stares at the floor. It looks like a lie. Innocent people squirm too.
chapters.counterintuition: It feels natural to read fidgeting as a sign of lying. But a squirm only shows that a question made someone uneasy, because honest people feel the same unease when they fear being doubted or blamed.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When someone looks uneasy, treat it as a reason to look closer, not proof they are lying.
chapters.tryThisNow: Tonight at dinner, when someone fidgets after one of your questions, wait a minute, then ask that question again gently.

memorableLines.text: A squirm marks the question to revisit, not the person to blame.

breakdown.fastRead:
Beatriz finds a crack across her tablet screen. She asks her son Tariq, fourteen, how it happened, and he rubs his palms down his jeans and stares at the floor. Has she caught him lying? If she says so and is wrong, he learns that honesty gets him nowhere.

Joe Navarro would say she has caught nothing yet. Spotting a lie is very hard, and even trained professionals do only a little better than a coin toss. Honest people show the same unease when they feel suspected. They reach for pacifying behaviors, small touches that calm the body, because they fear not being believed. A sign of discomfort is a flag. It shows you which topic to explore gently, not who is guilty.

Beatriz sits beside Tariq and asks about his day first. That gives her his baseline, how he acts when relaxed: chatty, hands moving. Then she comes back to the tablet, softly. He answers at once, nodding along. It was in her shopping bag on Saturday, he says, and last time something broke she blamed him before he could speak. She remembers the bag of potatoes she dropped on top. Accusing him would have made him squirm more. Stop reading a squirm as a confession, and let it point you to the question worth asking again, more gently.

breakdown.fullRead:
Beatriz finds a crack across her tablet screen. She asks her son Tariq, fourteen, how it happened, and he rubs his palms down his jeans and stares at the floor. Has she caught him lying? It certainly looks that way, and her gut agrees. If she says so and is wrong, he learns that honesty gets him nowhere. The next real problem in his life stays hidden from her.

Joe Navarro would say she has caught nothing yet. He warns that spotting a lie is very hard. Even trained professionals, he reports, do only a little better than a coin toss. If people whose job is catching liars do that poorly, a worried parent's gut deserves some doubt too.

The trouble is that honest people show the same signs when they feel suspected or stressed. To the limbic system, the part of the brain that reacts to danger before we think, being doubted is a threat. So an honest person under suspicion may reach for pacifying behaviors, small touches that calm the body, like rubbing the legs or stroking the neck. They may pull their arms in tight. They may turn the front of their body away, a move Navarro calls ventral denial. All of it can come from the fear of not being believed.

So Navarro does not hunt for the lie itself. He reads comfort against discomfort. Honest people tend to show comfort, and people who deceive tend to show discomfort, yet stress can make anyone squirm. Unease that shows up right after a question marks that question. It tells you where to look, not what you will find there. He treats it as a flag, a reason to look closer.

His way of looking closer is calm and slow. First, make the setting relaxed, so ordinary nerves can settle. Next, learn the person's baseline, how they act when nothing is wrong. Then ask your questions and notice where the unease rises. At that spot, watch whether words and body agree, such as a yes that comes with a nodding head. Watch for emphasis too. Truthful people tend to stress their points with their hands, or with gravity-defying gestures, moves that lift upward, like raised eyebrows. People who deceive tend not to.

Beatriz tries it. She sits beside Tariq and asks about his day first. He is chatty, his hands moving as he talks, and that is his baseline. Then she comes back to the tablet, softly, and asks when he last saw it. He answers at once, nodding along, his hands busy again as he explains. It was in her shopping bag on Saturday, he says. Last time something broke, she blamed him before he could speak. That was what the squirm had been about. Then she remembers the bag of potatoes she dropped on top of the tablet.

Her first reading would have misled her twice. The squirm was fear of blame, not a lie. And if she had pointed at him and demanded an answer, her own sharp tone would have made him squirm harder. The extra squirming would have looked even more like guilt, and an honest boy would have learned to stay quiet. Stop reading a squirm as a confession, and let it point you to the question worth asking again, more gently.

examples.title: A chipped bowl at the pottery studio
examples.scenario: Ezra's bowl has dried all week on the shelf at his Saturday pottery studio. Today its rim is chipped. He asks Wanjiru, who shares the shelf, if she moved it. A minute ago she was laughing and waving her hands. Now she wipes her clay hands on her apron, again and again, and turns toward her wheel. Ezra feels the word clumsy on his tongue.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the word back. Chat with Wanjiru about her own glaze for a minute, then ask softly when she last went near the shelf.
examples.whyItMatters: Her wiping shows the bowl worries her, not that she broke it, and a soft question keeps a studio friend talking.

examples.title: An apprentice chef who stopped speaking up
examples.scenario: Grete trains apprentice chefs. Last month she asked who had left the cold room open, and Nikhil stared at his shoes, picking at his thumb, so she blamed him. The real cause was a broken door latch. Today a tray of pastry has burned, and he is picking at his thumb again.
examples.whatToDo: Take Nikhil aside, ask how the rest of his week went, then ask calmly what happened with the oven and listen.
examples.whyItMatters: Last time the same signs came from fear of blame, so a calm question gives the real story a chance.

examples.title: A missing keyring as break ends
examples.scenario: Break ends in two minutes, and Freya is crying because her new unicorn keyring has gone from her bag. Aiko, her teacher, asks the children by the coat pegs if they saw it. Bilal goes red, squeezes his fingers and turns half away. The line is forming at the classroom door. Two girls are already whispering that Bilal took it.
examples.whatToDo: Say nothing about Bilal at the door. Settle the class, then kneel by his table once they are reading and ask quietly about break.
examples.whyItMatters: His unease points to break as the topic to explore, while a guess at the door could brand a child who may only fear blame.

questions.prompt: A cinema kiosk manager asks a new cashier, in front of the queue, whether she has been taking money from the till. The cashier flushes and rubs her arms. What happens as the manager keeps pressing?
choices: The cashier settles down once the hard question is over.
The cashier squirms even more, whether or not she took anything.
The cashier owns up soon, since her body has already given her away.
questions.explanation: A sharp question in front of a queue makes anyone uneasy, so the squirming grows whether she is honest or not. Her rubbing only shows the question hurt. It does not mean a confession is coming.

questions.prompt: Your friend says, "I asked my housemate about my missing headphones, and she went red and looked away. It was obviously her." What do you tell your friend?
choices: Ask her about them again, calmly, and see what she says.
Tell her plainly that you know, before the headphones vanish.
Drop it, since honest people blush too and it's not worth it.
questions.explanation: Going red shows the headphones are a touchy topic, not that she took them, so a calm second question is how to learn more. Dropping it throws away the clue her unease gave you.

questions.prompt: A rowing coach asks a boy why he missed Tuesday's session. The boy shuffles his feet and pulls his arms in tight. The coach chats about Saturday's race, then asks again quietly. The boy says he couldn't afford the bus fare. Why did the coach get the real answer?
choices: The chat lowered his guard, so he slipped up and gave himself away.
Asking softly let him say what had really made him uneasy.
The friendly chat cheered him up after a bad week.
questions.explanation: The boy was uneasy about the bus fare, not hiding a lie. The easy chat and the quiet second question let him explain. Nothing slipped out by accident; he simply no longer felt blamed.

questions.prompt: In a one-to-one, you ask a colleague why her report came in late. She starts twisting her lanyard and turns her chair a little away. What is your next move?
choices: Ask the same question again, more firmly, until you get a clear answer.
Chat about her other project, then come back to the deadline gently.
Move on to the next item, and leave the deadline alone.
questions.explanation: Her twisting marks the deadline as the touchy topic. Easing her back to calm, then returning gently, gives her room to explain. A firmer repeat would only add unease that looks like guilt.

questions.prompt: A father asks his teenage daughter where she went after school. She fidgets with her keys and looks down, so he grounds her for lying. She stops telling him anything. Where did he go wrong?
choices: Grounding her for too long when it was her first lie.
Asking about after school, when he could tell the question would upset her.
Taking her fidgeting as the answer, not as a reason to ask more.
questions.explanation: Her fidgeting only showed the question made her uneasy, which an honest teenager feels too when she expects blame. Asking was fine. Treating her unease as proof is what shut her down.

questions.prompt: A volunteer usher looked tense when asked about missing raffle money. The stage manager now sits with her in the empty foyer, talks about tonight's show, then gently asks what happened at the raffle table. What is this calm approach most likely to bring?
choices: Her account comes out clearer, since she no longer feels accused.
She guards every word, since the chat tells her a question is coming.
She stays tense, since a calm room can't ease worry.
questions.explanation: Much of her tension came from feeling suspected. A relaxed setting and a soft question take that pressure off, so whatever happened at the table is easier for her to tell.

questions.prompt: A friend who has just started interviewing job applicants tells you he marks down anyone who fidgets on a question, since it means they are hiding something. How do you answer him?
choices: Mark them down only if they fidget on more than one hard question.
Tell them you've noticed, so they get a chance to explain.
Note which question it was, and ask a calm follow-up on it.
questions.explanation: Applicants fidget from plain nerves, honest or not. The fidget only shows which question to explore, so a calm follow-up there learns more. Pointing it out to them would add pressure and more fidgeting.

reviewCards.front: When someone shifts and rubs their hands right after your question, that tells you ...
reviewCards.back: ... which topic to come back to gently. It does not tell you they lied, since honest people squirm when they feel doubted.

reviewCards.front: A club treasurer saw a member go red when asked about a missing kit bag, and banned him. The bag turned up in the minibus. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: The treasurer took the blush as proof. It only showed the question worried the member, and a calm follow-up would have kept his trust.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what should a squirm after a question mean to you?
reviewCards.back: Uneasy is not guilty. It means slow down and look closer at that topic, gently, instead of deciding they lied.

reviewCards.front: A new volunteer at your food bank tenses up and looks down when you ask why the tins were not counted.
reviewCards.back: Decide nothing yet. Chat about her shift first, then come back to the tins in a calm voice and listen to her reason.

reviewCards.front: Why can't a nervous answer on its own tell you someone is lying?
reviewCards.back: Because honest people feel the same unease when they think they are suspected, and even trained professionals do only a little better than a coin toss.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Using signs of unease to find the topic that needs a calmer second look, without deciding anyone lied.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I sit down to ask someone about something that went wrong, I start with an easy topic, and only then ask about the problem, calmly.
When I catch myself thinking someone is lying because they look nervous, I name the question that made them uneasy and ask it again, gently.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Today, notice one moment when someone shifts or fidgets right after a question. Note which topic it was, and hold off on deciding why.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, before a talk about something that went wrong, start with an easy topic. Then ask the hard question softly and see whether the unease still shows.
